newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil profit-taking frenzy rocks regional markets.
newsitem.headline: Brazil profit-taking frenzy rocks regional markets.

text.p: Brazilian stocks tumbled on Tuesday and took regional markets with them amid a profit-taking frenzy triggered by fears that speculative attacks on Asian currencies could spread to Brazil.

The Sao Paulo stock exchange was down eight percent in heavy late afternoon trade. The losses were extended to Argentina, Mexico and Venezuela, whose markets were looking to Brazil, not Wall Street, for direction.
"It's difficult to say anything right now. Everybody wants to leave through the same door, that's why the market is plunging," said John Carioba, a trader at Indusval brokerage in Sao Paulo.
Despite the sharp drop in share prices, Brazil's currency, the real, resisted downward pressure in the spot market, falling only slightly against the dollar.

Of all Latin American countries, Brazil is seen as the most likely to face a steep devaluation in the medium term because of a mounting current account gap, lax government spending controls and a currency that some observers say is overvalued by up to 20 percent.
Central Bank officials on Tuesday denied any plans to devalue the currency or change the existing foreign exchange regime.

Also, economists played down the markets' furious sell-off as an exagerated profit-taking bout that is taking advantage of an unprecedented rally in Brazilian stocks. Share prices have surged 80 percent in the first seven months of the year and market players said a correction was long overdue.

Economists noted that Brazil's macroeconomic picture, while not perfect, is in far better shape than Thailand's, whose de-facto devaluation two weeks ago planted the seed for this week's market sell-off.

"At this stage, it's a healthy warning, but not with the strength yet to have either systemic or contagion effects of substance," said Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs and Co Inc in New York.

Still, the prospect of a strong devaluation in Brazil, Latin America's largest economy, sent shivers through financial markets in neighboring countries. Among those most worried was Argentina, whose exports to Brazil would be seriously hurt by a devaluation in Brazil.
Argentine stocks plummeted 3.68 percent by late afternoon on rumors of an upcoming devaluation in Brazil.

Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez told a news conference in Washington that a sharp devaluation in Brazil was not in the works and that the currency woes now plaguing Thailand, Indonesia and other Asian countries would not hurt Latin America.
In Mexico, stocks were down 2.11 percent in late afternoon and some traders were already referring to a "devaluation in Brazil" as though it had taken place.
Currently the central bank aims for 7 to 8 percent depreciation of the real each year, effecting this through several mini-devaluations each month.
Surrounded by turmoil, the real slipped only 0.06 percent in the commercial foreign exchange market today to 1.0808 to the dollar.
Traders said the Central Bank has $59 billion in reserves and fiercely defends its currency bands, accounting for today's relatively peaceful dealings in the forex market.
